::: {.why}
Equal weighting is not a straw man, it is the thing your risk model has to justify itself against, and milestone 4 will not accept a comparison that quietly leaves it out.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Say what implicit bet equal weighting, inverse volatility and minimum variance each make, in terms of expected returns.
- State the condition under which minimum variance beats equal weighting, and check it on your data.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Work out what each benchmark assumes: equal weighting is optimal when expected returns and risks are identical, inverse volatility when Sharpe ratios are equal and correlations are equal, minimum variance when expected returns are equal. Write each one as the mean vector that would make it optimal.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Run the horse race properly with rolling out-of-sample windows: five portfolios including two optimised versions, reporting Sharpe, turnover and gross exposure. Then repeat on 50 and 100 assets to show how the ranking changes with dimension.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Add `equal_weight`, `inverse_vol` and `min_variance` to a new qlib/portfolio.py so the benchmarks are one call and there is no excuse for omitting them later.
:::
:::

## The running strategy

::: {.project}
qlib/portfolio.py starts with the three benchmark constructions. Every portfolio result for the rest of the year is reported next to them, which is the rule milestone 4 is graded on.
:::
